problem: Long-horizon navigation in unseen, partially observable environments requires recalling observations from far in the past. RNN/LSTM policies squeeze history into a fixed-size state and are hard to optimise with BPTT over long sequences. Map-like external memories (2D grids, fixed layout sizes, geometry-based write operations) build in rigid domain-specific structure, compress observations at write time, and still usually rely on RNN controllers.
motivation: Tasks such as patrolling, coverage and object search depend on remembering which areas were visited and what was seen hundreds of steps earlier. Attention-based Transformer encoder-decoders handle long, unordered inputs well in NLP. The authors therefore store every step's embedded observation without aggregation and defer all reasoning to attention at action time, without committing to a map structure.
key_idea: Store every embedded observation (image modalities + relative pose + previous action) as an unstructured set memory and use a Transformer encoder (self-attention over the memory) plus a decoder (current observation as query) to output Q-values/actions, trained with DQN and no BPTT.
insight: Keeping all observations separately and reading them through attention beats both fixed-state (LSTM) and single-layer attention with an LSTM controller (FRMQN); the gains are largest on memory-heavy tasks: coverage 102.5 cells vs 87.8 for LSTM and 83.2 for FRMQN. The design choices were each checked by ablation: (a) Attention over the memory is better than max-pooling it (SM+Pooling), especially on semantic search (74.2% vs 60.6% classes found). (b) Removing the self-attention encoder cuts search reward by 23.7 (Fig. 5b). (c) Performance keeps rising as memory capacity grows from 50 to 500 steps for coverage and search, while roaming saturates at about 300 (Fig. 5a). (d) Last action, relative pose and depth are the critical modalities; RGB and segmentation matter mainly for search. (e) FPS-based memory factorization makes cost linear with little or no loss; FPS centers beat sliding-window and static inducing points on coverage and search (Table 4). (f) A monotonic exponential temporal embedding is more robust to noisy dynamics than a sinusoidal one (Fig. 7).
method: Observation embedding: RGB, depth (+ valid-depth mask) and one-hot NYU40 segmentation (64x48 each) each go through a modified ResNet-18 (filters reduced 4x, stride 1 in the first two conv layers, no global pooling) to a 64-d vector. Pose and previous action go through 16-d FC layers. These are concatenated and passed through an FC layer to give psi(o).

Scene memory: a set M updated as M ∪ {psi(o)} at every step, with no geometric structure and no compression. At each step all poses are re-expressed in the current agent frame (egocentric). Each pose is normalised as (x/5, y/5, cos θ, sin θ, e^{-t}) so that temporal recency is encoded softly.

Transformer policy: the encoder is an AttBlock(M, M) self-attention over the memory. The decoder is an AttBlock(psi(o_t), Encoder(M)) with the current observation as query. Both use multi-head attention (8 heads), 128-d keys/values, and residual connections with LayerNorm. Two FC layers output Q-values, and the policy samples actions from softmax(Q) as a categorical distribution.

Memory factorization: the O(|M|^2) self-attention is replaced by AttBlock(M, AttBlock(M̃, M)), where M̃ is a compressed set of centers chosen by iterative farthest point sampling in feature space. This gives cost O(|M||M̃|), i.e. linear in memory size for fixed |M̃|.

Training: standard DQN with a replay buffer of 1000 episodes, refreshed every 500 iterations. Batches are 64 episodes; Adam with lr 5e-4. There is no BPTT. The embedding networks are first pre-trained with memory size 1 (no attention) and then frozen for all models; training stops when validation performance stops improving.

numbers_note: The benchmarks are custom SUNCG tasks (roaming, coverage, search), not standard navigation benchmarks. The evaluation protocol is 46 test houses x 10 episodes with a 500-step horizon. The ablations are reported only in figures: memory capacity (Fig. 5a), modality/encoder removal (Fig. 5b, with textual deltas such as −23.7 search reward without the encoder), found classes over time (Fig. 4), and noise robustness (Fig. 7). Table 4 is on the validation split with |M̃|=100.
results: SMT beats all baselines on all three SUNCG tasks. Coverage: reward 474.6 and 102.5 covered cells, vs Reactive 416.2/86.9, LSTM 418.1/87.8 and FRMQN 397.7/83.2. Search: SMT 74.2% and SMT+Factorization 75.0% of target classes found (3.65/3.69), vs FRMQN 70.2%. Roaming: reward 394.7, vs FRMQN 384.2 and LSTM 379.7. Memory factorization gives linear-time attention at little or no cost; it is even slightly better on search.
limitations: Evaluated only on synthetic SUNCG houses and custom reward-defined tasks (roaming, coverage, multi-class search). There are no standard goal-reaching benchmarks such as ObjectNav or PointNav, and no real robot.
Uses ground-truth rendered semantic segmentation and, in the main experiments, ground-truth relative pose. Noisy dead-reckoned pose is tested only in the appendix and degrades reward.

Memory grows linearly with episode length and full self-attention costs O(|M|^2); the factorization mitigates this but can lose some performance (roaming 376.4 vs 394.7). Embedding networks are pre-trained and then frozen rather than trained jointly.
